title: COMEBACK OR ELSE
description: A fictional K-pop group has kidnapped your AP Language expertise. Pick seven favourite lyrics, identify their devices, and explain why they work. Rubber-duck interrogations, hazy teaching flashbacks, a disastrous press interview, and your own debut lyric sheet. Seven rounds; roughly 15–20 minutes plus the four-question fare home. Comic peril and harmless foam-prop slapstick; no injuries or real performers.

quiz.prompt: The driver asks: Which distinction is accurate?
options: Anaphora repeats clause openings; alliteration repeats consonant sounds.
Anaphora means any repeated consonant; alliteration repeats a whole paragraph.
Both devices guarantee that an audience agrees.
quiz.explanation: We own… repeated across clauses is anaphora. Repeated consonant sounds in silk smiles sell are alliteration. Either can serve a purpose without guaranteeing a response.

quiz.prompt: The driver asks: In “You wanted silence; I became thunder,” which analysis is best supported?
options: There is no contrast because both clauses concern sound.
The sentence proves the singer literally controls the weather.
Silence and thunder form antithesis; becoming thunder also supplies a metaphor for loud resistance.
It is a simile because every comparison uses like or as.
quiz.explanation: One line can use more than one device. Contrast and metaphor work together here; accurate analysis connects both to the speaker’s defiance.

quiz.prompt: The driver asks: Which explanation correctly connects device, wording and purpose?
options: A million phone checks is a verified count; an unanswered song question is necessarily a survey.
A million checks exaggerates anxious waiting; “why are you still singing?” can challenge denial without requesting information.
Any large number proves a claim, and every question is hypophora.
Hyperbole always produces sadness, and rhetorical questions always produce agreement.
quiz.explanation: Hyperbole stretches scale for effect. A rhetorical question can challenge or provoke thought rather than seek information; context and audience matter.

quiz.prompt: The driver asks: When is “Perfect timing—you left on my birthday” verbal irony?
options: Only if its opening repeats three times.
Even when the speaker sincerely welcomes the departure and means the praise literally.
When the hurt, frustrated speaker uses apparent praise to convey criticism of the timing.
quiz.explanation: The intended meaning reverses the literal praise in that context. Comic props or an unhappy event alone do not establish verbal irony.
